{"id": "17:44/q08", "question": "What is the nature and extent of every thing's glorification?", "turns_on": "Whether glorification is conscious utterance, the objective testimony of createdness, obedient operation, or a mode embracing these; and whether 'every thing' has literal exceptions.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q08/p1", "position": "Every created thing actually glorifies God, including inanimate things.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes plants and animals; al-Nakhaʿī, Mujāhid, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, Sufis and others cite food, pebbles, wood, doors and water. Al-Qurṭubī prefers literal universality from reports and David's mountains; God can create life and speech. Bursawī calls this sounder if inanimate speech is possible. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it conscious disclosure without requiring phonemes; prophetic reports and 21:79, 38:18, 34:10 support it. Al-Ālūsī cites strong audible reports, yet finally reconciles it with state testimony. Abū Ḥayyān reports God granting speech to lifeless things; al-Rāzī records literal advocates' appeal to the otherwise incomprehensible praise. A damaged al-Thaʿlabī report has an unidentified thing praising for three hundred years; al-Durr reports one created thing praising whenever a servant does and ʿIkrima naming pillars and trees."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p2", "position": "Only living, ensouled, or growing things literally glorify; cut or dead material ceases.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda say living or spirited beings, including trees and plants. ʿIkrima says a tree does but a column does not; al-Ḥasan says a table once did. Yaḥyā reports severed stone and wood stop. Ibn Kathīr connects this with the fresh grave branches; al-Rāzī objects that treating inanimate matter as speaking while cut wood cannot is inconsistent. Al-Naḥḥās reports an unspecified restriction."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p3", "position": "Every thing glorifies through its created state as a sign of its Maker.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj's reported view and al-Wāḥidī say created things signify a wise, defect-free Creator; al-Zajjāj objects that pagans already admit the Creator. Al-Rāzī says inert things cannot know or speak, each apple part and attribute testifies to a determiner, and one verb cannot be literal and figurative at once. Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān similarly avoid double usage. Al-Biqāʿī cites origination, precision and passing; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that such evidence is already understood and misses conscious praise. Abū Ḥayyān reports the condition of inanimate things as metaphorical testimony; Ibn al-Jawzī calls the heavens' praise evidence of divine creation and power."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p4", "position": "Both verbal praise and testimony through created states are encompassed.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows a word to bear both senses; al-Biqāʿī assigns speech to capable creatures and signs to all. Bursawī and al-Ālūsī allow combined senses or a broad figure; al-Ālūsī prefers every thing's state and voice, with rebuke for missed testimony. Al-Rāzī and al-Kashshāf resist combining literal and figurative senses; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects dividing creation by mode."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p5", "position": "Creation glorifies by obedient submission to divine laws.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports submission as one explanation for inanimate things; Kur'an Yolu describes the cosmos' ordered operation and Raghib's distinction between voluntary conscious worship and universal obedience. The form can include human faith, acts, worship and morals."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p6", "position": "Each being manifests its distinctive perfection and seeks completion from God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī distinguishes skies' permanence and influence, earth's stability and nurture, angels' knowledge, and immaterial beings' transcendence. Bursawī transmits him; al-Ālūsī calls such state-praise accepted and repeats the examples."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p7", "position": "A report excludes donkeys and dogs from universal praise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is named in al-Durr and al-Ālūsī; al-Ālūsī doubts the attribution and sees no ground for preferring the exception to the unqualified reports."}, {"id": "17:44/q08/p8", "position": "At sunrise Satan and wealthy humans are excepted from all creatures' praise.", "reasons": "The report in al-Durr limits this exception to the sunrise event; it does not assert their exclusion at every time."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q09", "question": "What words or sounds are described as creation's glorification?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports convey a shared formula, a heaven-specific hymn, natural sounds, or a spiritual mode of speech.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q09/p1", "position": "Creation's prayer is 'Subḥān Allāh' or 'Subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi'.", "reasons": "Noah instructs his son or two sons to say it, and reports call it a means of provision; versions vary between formulas and deathbed setting. Ibn Kathīr says Jābir's chain through Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda is weak and a longer Aḥmad version is unique. Ibn ʿAmr's expanded remembrance has profession, praise, greatness, glorification and reliance. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains provision through manifest need."}, {"id": "17:44/q09/p2", "position": "Each heaven has its own hymn of praise.", "reasons": "Luṭ ibn Abī Luṭ's report assigns seven different formulas, from praise of the Most High in the lowest to majesty and dignity in the seventh. A Night Journey report has the Prophet hear the upper heavens praising the majestic exalted Lord; Ibn Kathīr gives no grade."}, {"id": "17:44/q09/p3", "position": "A creature's characteristic sound or act can be its praise.", "reasons": "Reports name a rooster's cry and wing motion, frog's croak, sea sound and waves, a door's creak, flowing water, cracking timber, and bird calls at dawn asking provision. A heavenly caller prompts a rooster; ʿAlī and al-Bāqir describe birds seeking daily food. Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes hearing these sounds from grasping their meaning."}, {"id": "17:44/q09/p4", "position": "Every creature may praise in its own tongue, including a heavenly or spiritual tongue.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān says different languages are heard by opened inner ears; al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says inanimate things use a heavenly tongue and each particle has a spiritual kingdom; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes real meaning from the words senses supply, like dream images."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q10", "question": "When, if ever, does a creature cease glorifying?", "turns_on": "Whether altered or dead matter stops praise, and how reports about cut or soiled things fit universal wording.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q10/p1", "position": "Glorification ceases when a thing loses life, original state, or freshness.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says cut stone, wood, and a former tree-table cease; Qatāda and al-Suddī say original things destined to die praise. Al-Miqdām's details vary by report: soil wetness, a bead's movement, a leaf falling, water changing, clothes becoming dirty or old, and animals no longer vocalizing. ʿĀʾisha is told to wash soiled clothes. Ibn Kathīr connects this with moist palm branches, but leaves the mechanism to God."}, {"id": "17:44/q10/p2", "position": "Birds, fish and hunted creatures lose praise before being caught or cut.", "reasons": "Reports link hunted game, caught fish, cut trees and branches to neglected glorification. Some specify that no fish or bird is taken before abandoning its prescribed praise. Abū Bakr remarks on the cause; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī records Shiʿi and Sunni routes. A report says an animal or insect lives until its praise ends, when God takes its soul; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says other angels mediate rather than the Angel of Death."}, {"id": "17:44/q10/p3", "position": "Glorification persists even in inert or altered material.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan reports soil glorifying after becoming a wall; other reports describe food, dry wood, house creaks, and a cooking pot praising. The universal-literal view does not condition praise on freshness."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q11", "question": "What reports show particular creatures praising or responding?", "turns_on": "Which particular report is being cited; the narrations differ in creature, scene and wording.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q11/p1", "position": "Food, water, pebbles, vessels, a tree trunk and a stone were heard or seen responding near the Prophet or others.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd reports food heard during the Prophet's meal and water from his fingers; al-Bukhārī contains the food account. Pebbles praise in hands of the Prophet and three caliphs, while variants differ over other Companions. Thaʿlabī reports grapes and pomegranates at a meal. Anas reports thārīd heard by several. Jābir ibn Samura says a Meccan stone greeted the Prophet before his mission, perhaps the Black Stone. Reports add a groaning trunk, a cooking pot and household vessels."}, {"id": "17:44/q11/p2", "position": "The Prophet heard the heavens praise during the Night Journey.", "reasons": "A report has him returning from Jerusalem and hearing the highest heavens glorify; Ibn Kathīr does not grade it. Another says every span of the weighty creaking sky holds an angel in prostration and praise."}, {"id": "17:44/q11/p3", "position": "David heard or was rebuked by the praise of other creatures.", "reasons": "Accounts describe David's mountains and birds, a frog with words David had never used, seventy thousand frogs standing on one leg, a more diligent night-praying frog, and a tiny pearl that rebukes his self-regard. Abū Mūsā says the red worm praises most. Some versions say a frog's praise surpassed David's."}, {"id": "17:44/q11/p4", "position": "Animals and places answer, remember, or testify.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd says mountains ask about human remembrance; Anas says regions of earth ask each other morning and evening, and creatures hearing the call to prayer testify. Reports describe ants praising and God rebuking a prophet who burned

{"id": "17:44/q12", "question": "What conduct toward creatures or graves follows from their praise?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse grounds etiquette toward praising creatures, benefit at graves, or reward for their caretakers.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q12/p1", "position": "Respect animals and avoid striking faces, overburdening mounts, and needless killing of frogs or ants.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima advises against insulting animals or garments. Prophetic and ʿUmar reports forbid face-striking; related reports forbid branding faces. Mounts may remember God more than riders, so riders should not use them as seats for conversation. Al-Sakūnī lists six mount rights including feeding and watering. Frogs' croaking is praise and ants form a praising community."}, {"id": "17:44/q12/p2", "position": "Fresh branches and recitation may benefit the dead.", "reasons": "The two-graves report says punishment for tale-bearing or backbiting and failing to avoid urine was hoped to ease until the palm branches dried. Some infer their ongoing praise caused relief. Al-Qurṭubī also supports planting trees and reciting Qur'an at graves, saying dedicated reward reaches the dead; Ibn Kathīr leaves the branches' mechanism to God."}, {"id": "17:44/q12/p3", "position": "A crop's glorification benefits the one who planted it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Qubayl say the reward of a praising crop goes to its owner or planter."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q13", "question": "Does inanimate glorification require life and awareness?", "turns_on": "Whether knowledge and speech presuppose ordinary life, another fitting life, or simply a created sound.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q13/p1", "position": "Actual praise can occur because God grants fitting life and knowledge to all things.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says God creates life and speech; Bursawī quotes Ibn ʿArabī on life throughout the world, the mountain knowing God's greatness, and audible praise being veiled. Al-Ālūsī adduces reports about all things testifying to the call to prayer, fever addressed as conscious, the moon, Nile and earth; awareness need not resemble animal sense. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says knowledge accompanies existence in proportion to it and true speech need not be phonetic."}, {"id": "17:44/q13/p2", "position": "God can make a stone speak by creating sound without giving it life.", "reasons": "Bursawī transmits al-Suhaylī's alternatives: create life and intelligence, or merely create the sound."}, {"id": "17:44/q13/p3", "position": "Inert matter lacks the life needed for knowledge and speech; its praise is evidential.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says otherwise the proof from knowledge and power to life would collapse; he also argues literal advocates inconsistently end a slaughtered animal's or broken branch's praise. Al-Ālūsī reports the Imam's parallel objection."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q14", "question": "Why do people fail to understand their glorification?", "turns_on": "Whether failure is due to a veiled language, neglected inference, the inexhaustible detail of signs, or a nonphonetic mode of conscious speech.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q14/p1", "position": "Its languages or speech differ from human language and are normally veiled.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Nasafī, al-Kawwāshī and others say humans do not know other beings' tongues. Al-Sulamī says opened hearts can hear them; al-Ḥasan says unveiling household praise would make normal living impossible. Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes hearing birds, thunder and frogs from understanding them. Bursawī objects that language difference alone cannot account for soundless beings; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects conventional human-like hidden words."}, {"id": "17:44/q14/p2", "position": "People neglect reflection on creation's testimony to God.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj's report says disbelievers miss the inference, but he objects that they already acknowledge creation. Al-Kashshāf, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr connect failure to defective reasoning and shirk. Al-Rāzī points to hidden countless apple parts and overlooked proofs of unity, justice, prophecy and resurrection; al-Biqāʿī says the wording is 'understand' rather than 'hear' because reflection is at issue. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects this contextual explanation."}, {"id": "17:44/q14/p3", "position": "God teaches its reality selectively, and human understanding remains incomplete.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj suggests God grants knowledge of praise; al-Baghawī entrusts the reality of inert things to God. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows that no person fully understands all details. Al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say uncounted parts and attributes each bear testimony; Kur'an Yolu likens the remaining unknown to the scale of atoms and genetic code. Al-Qāshānī says only an attentive living heart perceives the unseen."}, {"id": "17:44/q14/p4", "position": "Their conscious disclosure is real but need not take audible human words.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says true speech is any disclosure of inward meaning and that a hearer's senses may present it as words, like dream images. People already understand mere evidence of a Creator, so the verse points beyond it."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q15", "question": "Whom does 'you do not understand' address?", "turns_on": "Whether the rebuke follows the preceding polytheist argument, universal human limits, or the closing forgiveness.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q15/p1", "position": "It addresses polytheists or unbelievers who fail to infer God's transcendence.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj's objection is that they already accept Him as Creator; al-Kashshāf says they fail to follow that admission to its implication of no partners. Al-Ālūsī ties the address to the preceding false attributions, rejecting Ibn al-Munīr's interruption argument. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows this reading, as does Ibn ʿAṭiyya for heedless disbelievers."}, {"id": "17:44/q15/p2", "position": "It addresses people generally, because they cannot comprehend all praise.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports the universal addressee; Ibn al-Jawzī makes it follow literal praise. Bursawī reports a reading applying to Muslims and polytheists alike. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows that no human fully comprehends; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī does not require full comprehension."}, {"id": "17:44/q15/p3", "position": "It addresses believers who fail to hear inanimate speech.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Munīr argues that the closing forgiveness cannot address unrepeant polytheists, whose association God does not forgive; al-Ālūsī rejects this as disrupting passage coherence."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q16", "question": "What does fiqh add to the verb 'understand'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q16/p1", "position": "Fiqh is understanding that goes beyond bare knowledge, especially subtle or inferred knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says common usage restricts fiqh to inferred religious law, so God is not called faqīh. Al-Burhān says it exceeds simple knowing; Ibn ʿĀshūr says its choice over taʿlamūn signals subtle detail. Al-Sāmarrāʾī notes that audible praise still needs interpretation."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q17", "question": "Is another reading reported for 'you do not understand'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q17/p1", "position": "A passive intensive lā yufqahū is transmitted.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records it without further argument."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q18", "question": "What do ḥalīm and ghafūr mean in this closing?", "turns_on": "Whether the names are read as general patience and repentance, a temporal division, or a lexical contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q18/p1", "position": "God delays punishment for sin, shirk or heedlessness and forgives those who repent.", "reasons": "Muqātil says He overlooks partner claims until an appointed time; Qatāda contrasts divine patience with human haste. Ibn Kathīr cites 11:102, 22:48, 4:110 and 35:41–45: persistent rebels may be seized, repenters forgiven. The names also show His rule is undiminished and mercy costs Him nothing, says al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī. Kur'an Yolu defines ḥalīm as patient despite rebellion and relates it to other divine names."}, {"id": "17:44/q18/p2", "position": "Forbearance is in this life and forgiveness is for believers in the next.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī pairs worldly clemency with otherworldly forgiveness; al-Nasafī specifically says believers' sins are forgiven."}, {"id": "17:44/q18/p3", "position": "Ḥalīm is the opposite of foolishness.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives this lexical contrast."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q19", "question": "How do the closing words work grammatically and rhetorically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q19/p1", "position": "Ḥalīman is the accusative predicate of kāna.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives the parsing; Ibn ʿĀshūr says kāna presents both names as established and enduring attributes."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q20", "question": "Why does the verse end with forbearance and forgiveness?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate reason is failure to grasp signs, human disobedience amid sinless creation, or the prior declaration of transcendence.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q20/p1", "position": "God spares people who neglect signs, reason badly, and ascribe partners.", "reasons": "Muqātil cites the preservation of heavens and earth at 35:41; Yaḥyā cites 16:61, that immediate punishment would bring ruin. Al-Rāzī says culpable failure to infer fits these names better than inability to hear unfamiliar sounds. Al-Biqāʿī says a clear testimony makes neglect deserving of punishment. Al-Iṣlāḥī says the grave claim could bring down the heavens."}, {"id": "17:44/q20/p2", "position": "Creation praises sinlessly while humans disobey, so the names offer respite and pardon.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān and al-Itqān cite a report that grazing beasts, bowed elders and nursing infants ward off punishment. Al-B

urhān also links this with angels praising and seeking forgiveness for earth's people at 42:5; another al-Itqān view makes the names cover shortcomings of those praising God."}, {"id": "17:44/q20/p3", "position": "The ending connects God's transcendence with His merciful restraint.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports one reading attaching the names to 'transcendent' and another on respite despite lies; al-Ālūsī calls a proposed direct attachment weak. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the names show sovereign power and unharmed mercy."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q21", "question": "How does this verse connect to its context and other scripture?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is the local anti-shirk argument, the sūra's tasbīḥ wording, or supporting scriptural depictions.", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q21/p1", "position": "It completes the preceding rejection of partners: all dependent creation attests to its one Lord.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr contrasts universal praise with the claim of a divine child and cites 19:90–92; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says all creation comes from, depends on and returns to God. Kur'an Yolu and Study Quran connect it to 17:42 and created things' submission; al-Qurṭubī cites 38:17–18, 2:74 and 19:90–91. Al-Ṭabrisī says repeated proofs remove excuses although unbelievers flee."}, {"id": "17:44/q21/p2", "position": "It joins the sūra's recurring tasbīḥ language and the preceding 'Glory be to Him'.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says opening subḥān is timeless and unbounded and fits the sūra's tasbīḥ theme. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the universal-praise clause circumstantial to subḥānahu. Study Quran reports that some read 'Glory be to Him' as all creatures' universal prayer. Al-Ṭabrisī gives two ways of coordinating the preceding 'above what they say.'"}, {"id": "17:44/q21/p3", "position": "Other scriptures and verses depict creation's praise and God's restraint.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites Psalms 68, 85, 88, 95, 97, 148 and 150, ranging from heavens and seas to creatures, nations, stars and instruments; 148 lists their divinely set limits. He also says David's Psalms repeatedly commend reflection. Ibn Kathīr links 35:41–45 and 11:102 to delayed judgment. Muqātil cites thunder at 13:13; Study Quran cites 13:13, 13:15, 16:49–50 and 22:18."}, {"id": "17:44/q21/p4", "position": "Some related recitation and reflection notes concern the preceding verse's call to heed proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī discusses light/geminated li-yadhdhakkarū and says its point is reflection, not recalled memory, citing 28:51 and 38:29; he says Qur'anic repetition should induce recognition. Al-Sāmarrāʾī's presenter says grammatical and rhetorical mastery is needed to grasp such discourse; modern readers often lack the earlier Arabs' fluency."}]}
{"id": "17:44/q22", "question": "Why does this verse use min/man with those who praise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:44/q22/p1", "position": "Man marks those who glorify, while mā elsewhere gathers all things.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares 24:41 and the formulas in 59:24, 62:1, 64:1 and 57:1 to explain the wording."}]}
{"id": "17:83/q01", "question": "Who is the human described here?", "turns_on": "Whether the generic noun is unrestricted, contextually narrowed to unbelievers or Quraysh, or tied to a named occasion; al-Rāzī disputes the al-Walīd report.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q01/p1", "position": "Human beings generally, though the fault is strongest in unbelievers and does not include those God protects.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes sinners while saying the trait is strongest in unbelievers. Al-Rāzī cites 96:6–7 against restricting the verse to al-Walīd. Ibn Kathīr cites 10:12 and 17:67 and excepts those God protects. Al-Biqāʿī says exceptions are few, citing the prodigal of 10:12 and patient of 11:11. Al-Ālūsī says a generic species term can be true of only some members. Study Quran treats blessing and harm as a test of people generally (21:35)."}, {"id": "17:83/q01/p2", "position": "Unbelievers or polytheists specifically, despite the general wording.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls him an unbeliever, and Yaḥyā a polytheist. Ibn ʿAṭiyya points to the preceding wrongdoers; al-Ṭabrisī says unbelievers expect no reward for illness. Abū Ḥayyān compares other generic condemnations in 100:6 and 70:19. Kuranyolu points to the ẓālimūn of 17:82. Al-Qurṭubī identifies those whom the Qurʾān increases in loss."}, {"id": "17:83/q01/p3", "position": "Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is cited by al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and al-Rāzī; al-Qurṭubī says a report makes this the occasion. Al-Rāzī calls the identification far-fetched and instead applies the verse generally."}, {"id": "17:83/q01/p4", "position": "The Quraysh opponents who evaded God's Book and Messenger.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī takes the general noun as contextually referring to the Quraysh miscreants."}, {"id": "17:83/q01/p5", "position": "ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī identifies him in the verses about turning away after mercy."}]}
{"id": "17:83/q02", "question": "What blessing has God given the human?", "turns_on": "Whether the favor is material well-being or revealed guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q02/p1", "position": "Worldly ease, health, wealth, provision, rescue, victory, or removal of harm.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies provision, Yaḥyā ease and health, al-Māwardī health and wealth, Ibn al-Jawzī ample provision and relief, and al-Kashshāf health and prosperity. Al-Ṭabarī frames the favor as rescue from peril at sea after supplication; Ibn Kathīr adds victory and desired things."}, {"id": "17:83/q02/p2", "position": "Guidance offered to the person.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī's alternative makes the following aversion refusal to listen and accept."}, {"id": "17:83/q02/p3", "position": "The Qurʾān itself.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī gives this alternative, so the following turning away is from the Qurʾān."}]}
{"id": "17:83/q03", "question": "What does turning away describe?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of aversion is foregrounded: neglected devotion, rejected revelation, or pride.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q03/p1", "position": "Neglecting God's remembrance, supplication, worship, obedience, and gratitude after favor.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, and al-Baghawī stress ceasing prayer. Al-Ṭabarī says the rescued sea traveler acts as though he never called on God. Al-Rāzī says the face turns aside literally; al-Ṭabrisī says he neglects duties owed for blessing. Al-Ālūsī says he acts self-sufficient. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the omitted object is supplied by context: God, worship, commands, and prohibitions. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a saying about a believer turning away and God turning away from him."}, {"id": "17:83/q03/p2", "position": "Rejecting offered guidance, especially listening to and accepting the Qurʾān.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī makes guidance the blessing. Al-Nasafī offers the Qurʾān as the blessing. {"id": "17:83/q04", "question": "What does نأى بجانبه mean?", "turns_on": "Whether naʾy names distance, deliberate shunning, failed gratitude, arrogant posture, or inward refusal; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes the lexical equation of naʾy with buʿd.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q04/p1", "position": "He distances his whole person from God, leaving closeness to Him.", "reasons": "Mujāhid is repeatedly quoted as saying he moves far from God; Yaḥyā calls it equivalent to turning away. {"id": "17:83/q08", "question": "How is the reordered ناء form derived and understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the changed letter order is a metathesis of the distance root or a distinct root meaning rising or heaviness.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q08/p1", "position": "It is metathesis of naʾā, retaining the sense of moving away.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls it valid Arabic but less eloquent; al-Naḥḥās points to naʾaytu and raʾaytu rather than hypothetical naʾtu and raʾtu. {"id": "17:83/q09", "question": "How is يؤوسا pronounced when its hamza is eased?", "turns_on": "Whether easing hamza retains a consonant cluster or transfers the vowel to wāw.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q09/p1", "position": "The hamza may be dropped while leaving adjacent silent letters, an attested Arabic treatment.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares ولا يؤده حفظهما (2:255) and بعذاب بئيس (46:34) and says ordinary speech keeps the hamza-less cluster."}, {"id": "17:83/q09/p2", "position": "Readers transfer the hamza's vowel to wāw, yielding a yūsa-like form.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ reports this practice but calls it heavier and unattested in ordinary speech; al-Kisāʾī transmits يوسا and compares وإذا المودة to الموزة."}]}

{"id": "17:83/q12", "question": "Why does adversity make the person despair?", "turns_on": "Whether despair follows unbelief, guilt, delayed relief, reliance on causes, former ingratitude, or grief itself.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q12/p1", "position": "He lacks faith, trust in God's grace, or hope of recompense.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says he does not intend to seek recompense; al-Māwardī gives disbelief as one cause. {"id": "17:83/q17", "question": "Why is blessing attributed directly to God while evil merely touches the human?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q17/p1", "position": "Good is intended by divine generosity in itself; evil is not directly attributed because it is incidental or relative to its bearer.", "reasons": "Bursevī and al-Ālūsī note the asymmetry. {"id": "17:83/q18", "question": "What is evil and how does it arise under divine providence?", "turns_on": "The nature of evil as privation, limits of contingent matter, whether the whole order has predominant good, and the disputed relation of divine choice to necessity.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q18/p1", "position": "True evil is privation of an attainable good; positive harmful things count as evil through the loss they cause.", "reasons": "Philosophers reported by al-Ālūsī distinguish nonbeing such as poverty and ignorance from weather, vice, theft, or pain that obstruct good; fire perfects itself though it harms its victim, and revenge can perfect the irascible faculty. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes Plato's killing example: the evil is the victim's lost life, not the sword's sharpness or the killer's strength. He distinguishes absolute nonexistence from missing a fitting capacity, as in blindness."}, {"id": "17:83/q18/p2", "position": "Essential limits come from contingency; accidental loss of attainable perfection arises through matter and limited receptivity.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī's philosophical account says only God has absolute perfection; a thing's impossible perfections require no further cause, whereas loss of an attainable quality such as philosophy does. Material beings, unlike immaterial creations perfect for their kind, have prime matter and receptivity that permit such privation. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says a plant's lack of animal life follows its essence and is not created, while illness and pain arise in matter. God's decree wills a thing's attainable existence essentially; the accompanying lack follows limited capacity incidentally. Al-Ālūsī reports philosophers locating defects in contingent receptivity rather than divine stinginess."}, {"id": "17:83/q18/p3", "position": "Divine wisdom creates pure good and mixtures with more good than evil; evil-dominant or equal mixtures do not occur.", "reasons": "Philosophers reported by al-Ālūsī say pure, dominant, and equally balanced evil are absent; withholding goods of the elemental world to avoid rare harms would cause greater evil and deprive many beings. Al-Ālūsī says a small evil can beautify the whole like a dark beauty mark. He says God brings about what is free of evil or has little evil where absence would be worse, links the principle to 20:50, and points to al-Ishārāt and its commentaries. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also evaluates five possible balances and reaches pure or predominant good."}, {"id": "17:83/q18/p4", "position": "The inquiry presupposes a debate over divine choice, but philosophers can affirm God's choice and explain evil without dualism.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the analysis assumes a view of divine choice shared by Ashʿarīs, while philosophers relate choice to universal laws and wisdom; he rejects al-Rāzī's charge of pointlessness. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports al-Rāzī's analogy to fire's necessary burning, replies that necessity of the effect cannot compel its cause, and praises al-Ālūsī's fair account. He says philosophers investigate evil to avoid positing two principles, as Magians do."}, {"id": "17:83/q18/p5", "position": "Philosophical inquiry into evil is pointless if God acts by necessity rather than free choice.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes al-Rāzī's criticism comparing necessary divine action to fire burning; al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject it as partisan or biased."}]}

{"id": "17:83/q20", "question": "What inward reading is given to blessing and harm?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward obstruction is reliance on spiritual blessings or attachment to bodily and visible causes.", "positions": [{"id": "17:83/q20/p1", "position": "Enjoying obedience or relying on blessings can make a person turn from the Giver.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī through al-Sulamī includes the savor of obedience, settling into it, and reliance on it for protection; he names guidance, faith, gnosis, and divine friendship the greatest blessings."}, {"id": "17:83/q20/p2", "position": "Attachment to self and body veils the Real in prosperity and God's power in hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says material effects breed pride, while insight would see God's power in both states and answer with gratitude and patience."}]}

{"id": "17:86/q02", "question": "How can God take away what He revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether 'taking away' removes the already revealed material from people and books or takes the recipient in death and thus ends further revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:86/q02/p1", "position": "He could erase the revelation from memory and written copies, leaving no trace or accessible scripture.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām says nothing at all would remain. Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī citing Abū Isḥāq, al-Jishumī, Ibn al-Jawzī citing al-Zajjāj, and al-Ṭabrisī's three authorities specify hearts and books; al-Ṭabrisī includes the Prophet's and community's memories. Al-Rāzī calls such complete removal extraordinary and links it to the little knowledge of 17:85. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Būrsawī, al-Ālūsī, Asad, and Study Quran specify manuscripts and memories; al-Būrsawī calls it a hypothetical supposition, leaving the Prophet as before revelation, and al-Ālūsī distinguishes written forms from stored mental images. Al-Zamakhsharī, reported by Abū Ḥayyān, says the Prophet would know nothing of the Book. Elmalılı stresses the Qurʾān revealed through the Holy Spirit and preserved against trials.
